title: How to Display Data Badly
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through Howard Wainer's essay "How to Display Data Badly," which ran in the Commentaries section of *The American Statistician* and is assigned as a reading in Stat 243's graphics unit. It answers a narrow but useful question: everyone agrees a graph should show data, show it accurately, and show it clearly — so what, concretely, does it look like when each of those three goals is violated, and how would you recognize the failure rather than just feel that a graph is bad? The chapter assumes you can already make a bar chart, a line chart, or a table and have run into the vague advice "make it clearer." It does not assume you already know Tufte's vocabulary — data density, data-ink ratio, chartjunk, perceptual distortion — those are defined below exactly as the essay uses them. There is no accompanying slide deck or transcript for this reading; the chapter is a straight working-through of the paper itself. ## The three ways to fail Wainer starts from a definition: the aim of good data graphics is to display data accurately and clearly. That definition has three parts — (a) showing data, (b) showing it accurately, (c) showing it clearly — and each part gives an avenue for failure. Invert all three and you get twelve rules, "the dirty dozen," grouped under the three headings above. The framing is satirical (these are instructions for how to display data *badly*), but the diagnostic content is serious: two of the three failure modes come with an actual number attached, so "this graph is bad" turns into something you can compute. ## Showing too little, and hiding what you do show **Rule 1 — show as few data as possible.** Tufte's *data density index* (ddi) is the number of numbers plotted per square inch. It is trivial to compute and surprisingly informative: across popular and technical media Wainer finds a range from .1 to 362. A graphic from *Social Indicators III* (*SI3*), originally printed in four colors at 7" by 9", carries 18 numbers over 63 square inches — a ddi of $18/63 = .3$ — and this is not an outlier: the median *SI3* graph runs .6. A plot from Friedman and Rafsky (1981) in *JASA* shows 4 numbers in 8 square inches, ddi $=.5$, against a *JASA* median of 27; in the authors' defense, the point of that graph was only to show that a critic's suggested method of analysis had gone nowhere, and prose probably would have done the job as well. A graph with almost nothing in it looks embarrassingly empty, which risks the reader noticing there was nothing to say. The fix, if you are committed to bad display, is to fill the empty space with what Tufte calls **chartjunk** — nondata ink that hides the paucity of information. Wainer's example is a plot of Japan's labor productivity relative to the United States carrying one number per year for three years: sparse enough to leave a lot of blank space, which chartjunk conveniently covers. **Rule 2 — hide what data you do show, by minimizing the data-ink ratio.** This is the ratio of ink spent plotting the data to the total ink in the graph; the closer to zero, the worse the graph. Two standard tricks: hide the data in the grid (make the grid fine and the plotted points dim, so the eye lands on the grid rather than the points), or hide it in the scale, by "zooming out" so far that real variation is swamped by the size of the axis — justified, if pressed, by an appeal to "honesty requires starting the scale at zero." An *SI3* plot of the number of private schools uses exactly this trick to bury a real jump in growth during the mid-1950s; redrawn on a scale that shows the variation, the rise becomes visible and raises an obvious question about its relationship to *Brown v. Topeka School Board*. ## Distorting the metaphor A graphic works because a set of numbers, with magnitudes and an order, is represented by a visual metaphor whose own magnitude and order are supposed to match. Rules 3 through 5 compromise that match in three different ways. **Rule 3 — ignore the visual metaphor altogether.** If the data are ordered and the visual metaphor has a natural order, shuffle the two: in one example a bar labeled 14.1 is drawn longer than a bar labeled 18. A subtler version changes what the metaphor *means* partway through the graphic — one example shades imports on one side of an axis and exports on the other, then changes the scale in the middle of the plot as well. William Playfair solved the same import/export comparison two hundred years earlier (1786) with a pair of clean, separate plots; two such plots here would have told the story without the sleight of hand. **Rule 4 — only order matters, not magnitude.** Use *length* as the visual metaphor when the reader will perceive *area*. *The Washington Post* did this well (badly) in a graphic with a ddi of .1 and a data-ink ratio near zero, showing the falling value of the dollar from Eisenhower to Carter. Tufte's **perceptual distortion** (PD) measures exactly this: the perceived change in the quantity, divided by the actual change. Reading the actual dollar values and the sizes on the page gives $$\text{Actual} = \frac{1.00 - .44}{.44} = 1.27 \qquad \text{Measured} = \frac{22.00 - 2.06}{2.06} = 9.68$$ $$\text{PD} = 9.68 / 1.27 = 7.62$$ — a distortion of over 700%, "substantial but by no means a record." PD is a general recipe: it applies wherever a graphic's visual size and the underlying number diverge, not only to this one example. **Rule 5 — graph the data out of context.** Choose the displayed interval to hide a drop (start the series just after it) or to turn a slight meander into a dramatic swing (crop to a single meander and expand the scale). Wainer's example is a Reagan-administration graphic of the effects of a tax cut shown out of context, against a *New York Times* redrawing that restores the surrounding history. Omitting both the context *and* the quantitative scale at once is the recipe for what Wainer calls "Ordinal Graphics" — and, he adds, no automatic rule catches all of this; it still takes judgment to notice. ## Obscuring what's shown The next six rules don't hide or distort the data outright — the numbers are there and may even be accurate — but subtle choices bury the point the reader most needs. **Rule 6 — change scales in mid-axis.** This can make a large jump look small, or an exponential curve look linear. A graphic supporting a story about circulation of the *New York Post* "skyrocketing" past the *Daily News* hides a 700,000 jump in exactly where the axis scale changes; it takes a careful look to find it. A plot of physicians' incomes over time looks nearly linear with a slight recent tapering — until you notice the x-axis starts by plotting every eight years and ends up plotting every year, which compresses the early, faster-looking growth and stretches out the recent, slower-looking growth. Redrawn on a regular scale, the story changes. **Rule 7 — emphasize the trivial, ignore the important.** A page from *SI3* compares men's and women's income by education level across time. The genuinely interesting comparison — the pay gap between the sexes *within* an education level — has to be made by mentally transposing information across two separate graphs, error-prone and awkward. The dataset has two large main effects (education, sex) and one small one (a mild trend over time); the fix is to make the two big effects easy to compare directly and push the small time trend into the background, not the reverse. **Rule 8 — jiggle the baseline.** Comparisons are easiest from a shared baseline; stacking removes one. Wainer's example is a USDA chart of red meat imports where shading beneath each line indicates running summation: each meat's amount is added to the ones below it. Because beef and veal dominate and fluctuate, it becomes hard to tell whether pork imports are rising, falling, or flat — its band's *top edge* is pushed around by whatever beef is doing underneath it, even if pork itself is moving steadily. Stacking's only real purpose is to make the total easy to read, and that can be had directly, with an explicit total line, while every component is drawn from its own common zero baseline. **Rule 9 — order alphabetically ("Austria First!").** Alphabetizing a table or a set of bars obscures whatever structure would have been visible under a data-driven order; the usual defense — "it aids lookup" — is only relevant for long lists, where nineteenth-century statistical-atlas indexing schemes already solved the lookup problem without sacrificing order. An *SI3* graph of life expectancy by sex across ten industrialized nations, listed alphabetically (with the USSR under "Russia"), delivers only "not much variation, women live longer." Reordered by magnitude — effectively a stem-and-leaf layout with spacing proportional to the actual differences — the size of the sex gap becomes obvious, and the USSR stands out as an outlier for men. **Rule 10 — label (a) illegibly, (b) incompletely, (c) incorrectly, (d) ambiguously.** A 1978 *New York Times* graphic on falling travel-agent commissions after airline fare cuts shows a small bar for the decline — with a tiny label revealing it covers only the first half of 1978, omitting the heaviest travel months (Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas). Simply doubling that half-year figure reverses the apparent story: agents were doing well. **Rule 11 — more is murkier: more decimal places, more dimensions.** A table from Dhariyal and Dudewicz (1981, *JASA*) reports optimal-selection values to five decimal places, far beyond what a reader can use or the analysis can justify. Rounded, the same table not only reads more clearly but reveals a redundancy across its columns — the maximum expected gain at $b/c = 10$ is roughly a tenth of the gain at $b/c = 100$, and a hundredth of the gain at $b/c = 1{,}000$: | $N$ | $r^*$ ($b/c{=}10$) | $G$ | $r^*$ ($b/c{=}100$) | $G$ | $r^*$ ($b/c{=}1{,}000$) | $G$ | | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | | 3 | 2 | .2 | 2 | 2.2 | 2 | 22 | | 4 | 2 | .3 | 2 | 2.9 | 2 | 29 | | 5 | 2 | .3 | 3 | 3.5 | 3 | 36 | | 6 | 3 | .4 | 3 | 4.2 | 3 | 43 | | 7 | 3 | .4 | 3 | 4.9 | 3 | 49 | | 8 | 3 | .5 | 4 | 5.6 | 4 | 56 | | 9 | 3 | .6 | 4 | 6.3 | 4 | 63 | | 10 | 4 | .6 | 4 | 6.9 | 4 | 70 | Extra plotted dimensions cause the same kind of murkiness graphically: once a bar chart becomes a three-dimensional object, it's ambiguous whether length, area, or volume carries the value, and human perception of areas and volumes is unreliable to begin with. Wainer's favorite instance of this is a per-share earnings and dividends chart where the 3-D bar for one year is drawn so that only its *side* is visible — apparently confusing the artist too, since the visible bars appear to be mislabeled by a year, with the true final year left unlabeled altogether. A plain two-dimensional line chart with the corrected years removes the ambiguity entirely. ## The last rule, and the counterexample **Rule 12 — if it has been done well in the past, think of another way to do it.** Color adds more misusable parameters. The U.S. Census's two-variable color map, which varies color saturation to encode two quantities at once, is a well-known source of confusion; Mayr solved the same two-variable-map problem a century earlier (1874), and more gracefully, using bars of varying width and frequency instead. Having spent the essay cataloguing failures, Wainer closes by pointing at what good practice looks like: hours spent with the six books of graphs William Playfair published between 1786 and 1822 — clear, accurate, and dense with data — repay themselves. His nominee for "World's Champion Graph" is Charles Minard's 1861 depiction of Napoleon's 1812 Russian campaign, reproduced from Tufte's book. Wainer quotes Tufte's description of it directly: > Beginning at the left on the Polish-Russian border near the Niemen River, the thick band shows > the size of the army (422,000 men) as it invaded Russia in June 1812. The width of the band > indicates the size of the army at each place on the map. In September, the army reached Moscow, > which was by then sacked and deserted, with 100,000 men. The path of Napoleon's retreat from > Moscow is depicted by the darker, lower band, which is linked to a temperature scale and dates at > the bottom of the chart. It was a bitterly cold winter, and many froze on the march out of > Russia. As the graphic shows, the crossing of the Berezina River was a disaster, and the army > finally struggled back to Poland with only 10,000 men remaining. Also shown are the movements of > auxiliary troops, as they sought to protect the rear and flank of the advancing army. Minard's > graphic tells a rich, coherent story with its multivariate data, far more enlightening than just > a single number bouncing along over time. Six variables are plotted: the size of the army, its > location on a two-dimensional surface, direction of the army's movement, and temperature on > various dates during the retreat from Moscow. ## What the measures have in common The essay's closing point is that its measures are not independent diagnostics but interlocking ones: data density cannot stay high once a graph is cluttered with chartjunk; the data-ink ratio rises automatically with the amount of real data shown; perceptual distortion shows up precisely where an extra dimension or an ill-chosen visual metaphor was used. The positive advice this collapses to is correspondingly simple: know what the data have to say before you draw anything, then let them say it with a minimum of adornment, keep the scale regular, label completely — and spend real time with the masters of the craft, since an hour with Playfair or Minard teaches more than another rule would. ## Sources - Howard Wainer, "How to Display Data Badly," Commentaries section, *The American Statistician* (received September 1982, revised September 1983). Read from the model-reconstructed markdown version used identically in three offerings of Berkeley Stat 243's graphics unit: `stat243-fall-2021/units/wainer1984.md`, `fall-2024/units/graphics_files/wainer1984.md`, and `fall-2025/units/graphics_files/wainer1984.md` — all three are the same text; this chapter is drawn from the fall-2021 copy (licensed CC0-1.0). - This chapter covers the entire supplied input: no slide deck, transcript, or exercise set accompanied this reading, only the paper itself. - The source markdown carries its own fidelity caveat, which this chapter inherits: it was reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no extractable text layer, the prose is a paraphrase in places, and every equation (including the perceptual-distortion calculation reproduced above) is unverified against the original typesetting. - The essay refers to 25 numbered figures (bar charts, the meat-import chart, Minard's graph, and others) that were not reproduced in the source conversion with captions tied to specific rules, so this chapter describes them from the surrounding prose rather than reproducing them. The Rule 8 diagram above is accordingly a schematic illustration of the argument, built with illustrative numbers, not a redrawing of the original chart or its data. - Works the essay itself cites and that a reader wanting the primal sources would need to chase down separately: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (1983), for the data density index, data-ink ratio, and chartjunk; Dhariyal and Dudewicz (1981, *JASA*) for the optimal-selection table; Friedman and Rafsky (1981, *JASA*) for the sparse two-sample plot; Playfair's *Commercial and Political Atlas* (1786) and later atlases (1786–1822); and Minard's original 1861 campaign graphic, as reproduced in Tufte (1983, p. 40).
